entry.title: Winding Yarn (Interior of a Nantucket Kitchen)
entry.blurb: Eastman Johnson was a cofounder of the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York.

source.credit: The Cleveland Museum of Art. Hinman B. Hurlbut Collection

facts: At the time, winding yarn was a common symbol of courtship that carried humorous overtones of a woman ensnaring her suitor.
The second woman in the composition is likely a chaperone.
The suitor’s unrefined, open-legged pose, coupled with his rude action of placing his hat on the floor, adds further comic elements that contemporary audiences would have appreciated.

candidate.title: Winding Yarn (Interior of a Nantucket Kitchen)
candidate.credit: The Cleveland Museum of Art. Hinman B. Hurlbut Collection
candidate.description: Set in a rustic kitchen on Nantucket Island, Massachusetts, this painting depicts a woman who winds a ball of yarn from a coil looped in the hands of a man sitting across from her at a respectable distance. At the time, winding yarn was a common symbol of courtship that carried humorous overtones of a woman ensnaring her suitor. The second woman in the composition is likely a chaperone. The suitor’s unrefined, open-legged pose, coupled with his rude action of placing his hat on the floor, adds further comic elements that contemporary audiences would have appreciated. Eastman Johnson was a cofounder of the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York.
